opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it matters in a few different ways, and some of them push in opposite directions.

The most direct effect is that inference-time compute gives you another axis for scaling capabilities. Historically the story was mostly "train a bigger model on more data." Now with reasoning models, you can also get substantial gains by letting the model think longer, sample many attempts, and select the best one. For AI R&D specifically, a lot of the work is verifiable to some degree. You can run the experiment, check whether the loss went down, check whether the code passes tests. That's exactly the kind of setting where spending more inference compute pays off, because you can generate lots of candidates and filter them.

So one implication is that the point where AIs can meaningfully automate research engineering might come earlier than you'd guess from the base capability trend. You might not need a model that's reliably as good as a top researcher on every attempt. You might just need one that's good enough sometimes, plus enough compute to run it many times and a decent way of checking the output.

The flip side is cost. If you only reach human-level research performance by burning a huge amount of inference per task, then at first the automation might not be much cheaper than just hiring people, or it might only make sense for certain narrow tasks. So you could get this regime where it's technically possible to automate a lot of AI R&D but it's compute-bottlenecked, and the labs have to trade off between using compute for running AI researchers versus using it for the training runs and experiments themselves. That could slow down the initial takeoff relative to a world where capable models were cheap to run.

But I don't think that regime lasts very long. Inference costs for a given capability level have been dropping really fast, through algorithmic improvements, distillation, better hardware. And crucially, once you have AIs doing a meaningful fraction of research, some of what they work on is exactly making inference more efficient. So you get a feedback loop: expensive initial automation, which then gets used partly to make the automation cheaper.

There's also a subtler point: inference compute lets you convert compute into something like serial research progress. Instead of needing more and more human researchers, which you can't scale quickly, you can just run more copies, run them faster, or let them think longer. That changes the bottleneck. In a human-driven world, the binding constraints are things like the number of talented researchers and how fast they can iterate. In an AI-driven world, it's much more about how much compute you have and how efficiently you allocate it between experiments and cognitive labor. That makes compute even more central to who's ahead, and it means takeoff speed depends a lot on how much compute a lab has already built up when it crosses that threshold.

From a safety perspective, I think this is a mixed picture. On one hand, inference-heavy approaches with visible chain-of-thought give us some transparency, because a lot of the reasoning happens in tokens we can at least partly read and monitor. That's quite valuable for control. On the other hand, it potentially means the transition from "AI is a useful tool for researchers" to "AI is doing most of the research" could be faster and more compute-driven than people expect, which leaves less time to get safety measures in place. So I think it raises the importance of preparing control and monitoring techniques now, before we're in that regime.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think inference compute matters a lot here, and it changes the picture in a few different ways.

The first thing is just that when we talk about automating AI R&D, the thing we care about is something like: how much useful cognitive labor can you get out of the compute you have? And historically people mostly thought about that in terms of training. You train a bigger model, it's smarter, it can do more. But now there's this other dimension where you can take a given model and spend much more compute at inference time, by having it think longer, run more attempts, do search, check its own work, and get substantially better performance. So you've got two knobs instead of one.

What that means is that the point at which you can automate AI research is probably somewhat earlier than you'd naively think from looking at training compute alone, because you can trade off. If the model is a bit below the threshold where it can do the task reliably, you can throw more inference compute at it and maybe get over the threshold.

But there's a flip side, which is that if you're relying heavily on inference compute to get the capability, then the number of effective researchers you can run in parallel is lower. A lot of the story for why AI R&D automation would be so explosive is that you'd have, you know, millions of copies running at many times human speed. If each copy needs to spend ten or a hundred times as much compute to actually be competent, then you've got correspondingly fewer of them, or they're slower. So you might hit "AI can do the research" earlier, but the initial speedup over human researchers is smaller than it would otherwise be, and then it ramps as you get efficiency improvements.

I actually think this makes the takeoff somewhat smoother in expectation. Rather than going from "can't do it at all" to "can do it with a huge amount of parallel labor," you have this intermediate regime where the AIs are expensive and you're carefully deciding where to spend the compute. And one of the main things they'd be spending it on is making themselves cheaper, because algorithmic progress that reduces inference cost immediately multiplies how much labor you have.

Another consideration is that AI R&D is a domain where inference compute is particularly useful. It's a lot of running experiments, iterating, checking results, and these are things where you can verify outcomes to a reasonable degree. So the test-time compute approaches that work well on math and coding should transfer pretty well. Which again points toward earlier automation.

The thing I'd flag as uncertain is how inference scaling trades off against the compute you'd otherwise want for experiments. In an AI lab, compute is the scarce resource, and if your automated researchers are eating a big chunk of it just to think, that's compute you're not using to run the training runs they're proposing. So there's a real tension there, and I think how that resolves depends a lot on how quickly inference costs fall. My guess is they fall fast, because that's exactly the kind of problem these systems would be pointed at.

So overall, I'd say: somewhat earlier onset, a somewhat less abrupt initial jump, but not fundamentally changing the picture that once you can substitute AI labor for human researchers, things can move very quickly.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes automation of AI R&D more plausible, though there’s a pretty important question about what the models are spending that compute doing.

One way to use more inference compute is to try lots of approaches and then select the ones that work. That’s particularly useful when you can check the result: you can run the code, run an experiment, or measure whether a change improves performance. A lot of AI research has that structure, so you could get substantial progress from models that aren’t consistently producing good ideas, but produce useful ideas often enough and can test them cheaply.

The harder part is that not everything is easy to check. An experiment might give you a misleading result, or improve some narrow metric without helping with the thing you actually care about. And deciding which research directions are worth pursuing can require judgment over quite a long horizon. So being able to spend more compute doesn’t automatically solve the whole problem.

But it does change the economics. You don’t necessarily need a model that can do research at the same speed or with the same number of attempts as a human. You need a system that produces useful research at a competitive cost. If additional inference compute lets you cross that threshold, then you can start using AI labor to improve the next generation of AI systems. How large an effect that has depends on what remains bottlenecked by experiments, training compute, and human oversight.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes automating AI R&D look more plausible, particularly if you can use additional inference compute to get models to work reliably on longer tasks. There’s a big difference between a model that occasionally has a good research idea and a system that can take an idea, implement it, run experiments, notice what went wrong, and iterate until it has a useful result.

One reason inference compute could help is that a lot of AI research has feedback you can check. You can run the code, see whether the experiment worked, and compare the result to a baseline. So you can potentially have models try multiple approaches and spend more effort investigating the promising ones. You don’t need every attempt to be good if you can cheaply identify the attempts that are good.

But I’d distinguish that from assuming you can just run a model for a hundred times longer and get a hundred times as much research. The attempts might all make similar mistakes, or the model might be missing some conceptual understanding that more time doesn’t fix. And experiments themselves take compute, so generating more ideas isn’t necessarily the bottleneck.

Overall, though, it gives you another way to improve these systems without waiting for a larger pretrained model. And once a system is reasonably close to being useful at AI research, being able to spend more compute on difficult steps could make a substantial difference to how much of the process you can automate.
